prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, trapping neutral atoms at the magic wavelength to bring frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep B013 alone, Katori and Ye, and my confidence has gone up since round 1 because the main objection fell away on a factual point. I wrote that Ye shared the 2005 prize. That was wrong: Glauber, Hall and Hänsch shared it, and Ye was Hall's collaborator. Danielsson, Kroll and Mehlig each said so, and I withdraw the statement. The case rests on measurement criteria I use in my own field. Katori's magic-wavelength trapping cancels the light shift while thousands of atoms sit in the Lamb-Dicke regime. Ye's group then brought systematic uncertainty to about 1e-18 with stability no single-ion clock matches. Independent laboratories (RIKEN and Tokyo, JILA, SYRTE, PTB, NIST) now compare clocks at that level, which is the calibration-and-systematics test I trust. The physics reach is concrete: gravitational redshift over millimetres, bounds on drifting constants, dark-matter searches and relativistic geodesy. On the chair's first question, the distinct achievement is many-atom interrogation with a cancelled light shift. The 2005 prize gave a frequency ruler and the 2012 prize gave control of single ions; neither delivered that. I would word the citation around the lattice and the magic wavelength, not around timekeeping in general. That answers Olsson's question on whether we reward the original work, since it names the invention and its realization together.
statement.case_against: Three reservations remain. First, support for B013 may reflect clean attribution more than top scientific weight. I still think the Higgs discovery carries more weight, and I would be uneasy if the committee chose the clock only because it is the easiest to write. Second, Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto, Derevianko, Oates and the SYRTE, PTB and NIST groups made real contributions that a two-name credit leaves out. Lindroth gives the early priority as Katori's proposal and first demonstrations in 2001-2003 and Ye's record realization, and I cannot check that from outside atomic physics. Third, the redefinition of the second has not happened, so the largest payoff is still ahead. I do not think that argues for waiting: the evidence base is already mature, and the prize should rest on delivered, reproduced measurements, not on a metrological decision still to come.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the 2005 prize rewarded the comb as a ruler and the 2012 prize rewarded control of single ions, while the lattice clock rests on many-atom interrogation with a cancelled light shift, and that the citation should be written around the invention and realization, with Lemonde and others secondary.
responses.response: I accept this and it is the distinctness argument I will defend in the committee room. I agree with your preference to word the citation around the invention rather than add names, since a third name is available only by dropping one of the two decisive ones. I also take your point that a prior-laureate objection does not hold, and I have corrected my own error on Ye. Where I stay cautious is the Higgs: your preference for checkable uncertainties is met by the clock, but it does not make the clock the more important result, and I think the committee should say so openly.

responses.point: Olsson asks whether Katori and Ye are credited for one achievement or two separable contributions, and says the prize should reward the original work and not a second group that did it much better.
responses.response: I would answer that the citation covers one achievement with two decisive steps: Katori's concept and first demonstration, Ye's drive to record accuracy and many-body stability. Lindroth's account of the 2001-2003 priority supports this reading. I would not split it into two prize parts, because that would put three people on a single field with no gain in clarity. I share your caution about rewarding a refinement, which is why I want the citation to name the invention and the magic-wavelength trapping first and the accuracy result second. I would ask you to say if the wording I propose still reads to you as a lifetime award for Ye.

responses.point: Danielsson keeps the Event Horizon Telescope (B016) and moire matter (B046) as the candidates that change how we picture the world, and says the clock is useful rather than existential.
responses.response: I understand the pull of a new picture of the world, and it is the reason I opened with a new-window candidate myself. Still, millimetre-scale redshift and bounds on drifting constants do test how time behaves in nature, so I would not call the clock only useful. On the EHT I stay where I was: I cannot support omitting Zensus, and a three-name EHT credit would still leave out a collaboration of hundreds, so for this year it fails on attribution, not on science. I would be glad to take B016 up again once polarization and dynamics results mature.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked magic-angle graphene first at opening, moved to B013 after reading the other ballots, and keeps B046 as an alternative while noting that the superconducting mechanism is unsettled and that Cao cannot be credited.
responses.response: Your own move to B013 is the most informative one for me, because it came from someone who values surprise over technique and who defers to atomic colleagues. I agree that B046 is a real field and that the continuum prediction was tested quantitatively, but I would not use it as a second part: a Bistritzer, MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero trio leaves out the first discoverers of the phases, and with two names already used for B013 we could add only one person. I do not think the mechanism question is the main obstacle, but the experimental credit is.

responses.point: Mehlig argues that the prize should rest on what is new, namely magic-wavelength cancellation and the 1e-18 regime, and not on the clock as a natural next step in a metrology series.
responses.response: I agree and I will not argue the case as a series. Your point that the mechanism is simple and general is the best reply to the sceptic: the magic wavelength is one principle that makes many-atom interrogation possible. On KPZ, I cannot judge the statistical-mechanics side, but credit by Kardar and Zhang with Takeuchi alone omits the exact-solution work you and others have raised, and you give it no more than alternative status yourself.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept that Katori and Ye stand for the achievement while Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto, Derevianko and the SYRTE, PTB and NIST groups are named in the discussion but not in the citation; I rely on Lindroth for the early priority dates.

Whether the Higgs experimental discovery (B001) should be set aside only because the three-name limit forces an arbitrary choice among Gianotti, Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee, and whether a prize for it should wait for a solution that the collaborations accept.
Whether IceCube (B059) has matured enough on source identification beyond the diffuse flux, and how Halzen, Karle and Spiering should be weighed against AMANDA, DUMAND and Baikal pioneers.
Whether the redefinition of the second, once decided, will change how the clock prize is read; I do not think support should depend on it, but Kroll and Olsson do.
statement.conflict_note: I am a member of the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations and work in astroparticle physics, adjacent to B059 (IceCube) and B016 (Event Horizon Telescope), which are only my alternatives or points of discussion. I have no personal or institutional tie to Katori, Ye or the other credited individuals and no recusal-level conflict for B013 or B001. I note Johansson's stated recusal on B054 and Olsson's possible recusal on B015, and I would treat their statements on those candidates as disclosed interests; neither affects B013. In round 1 I wrongly said Ye shared the 2005 prize; that is corrected here.
